title: My head hurts
goal: Describing pain, going to the doctor and buying medicine — while mastering the *-аа / -ээ* suffix, which means "one's own".
bekal: name body parts and say which part hurts
describe symptoms to a doctor and understand instructions for taking medicine

dialogs.title: Яриа — Эмнэлэгт
dialogs.intro: Budi has caught a cold after three days of wild weather swings. Sarnai takes him to the campus clinic.

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: Good afternoon. Where does it hurt?
lines.literal: well is Q. where your hurt-ing is Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: My head hurts. My throat too.
lines.literal: head my hurt-ing is. throat also too.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Three days now. I can't sleep properly at night.
lines.literal: three day become-ing is. night well sleep-ing able-not is.

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.literal: fever-ing is Q? cough-ing is Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: A slight fever. I think I've caught the flu.
lines.literal: little degree fever-ing is. flu reached probably.

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: Open your mouth. OK, your throat is red.
lines.literal: mouth-own-object open-please. OK, throat your red-become is.

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: Not serious. An ordinary flu. You'll be better in three or four days.
lines.literal: serious not. ordinary flu. three, four day-in heal.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Do I need to take medicine?

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: Yes. Take this medicine three times a day, after meals.
lines.literal: yes. this medicine-object day-in three time, food's after drink-please.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: I see. What else should I do?
lines.literal: understood. other what do must Q?

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: Drink plenty of warm fluids. Rest at home, and don't stay out for long.

lines.speaker: Эмч:
lines.id: You're welcome. If you're not better in three days, come back.
lines.literal: no-matter. if three day's after good-not if again come-please.

notes: ⚠️ **The suffix -аа / -ээ / -оо / -өө means "belonging to the subject of this sentence".** *Амаа ангай* = "open **your own** mouth"; *гэртээ амар* = "rest at **your own** home". It's like English "own", but used far more often: it attaches **after** the case suffix, and leaving it out makes your sentence sound broken.

**Compare these two sentences:** *Тэр гэр**тээ** харьсан* = "He went back to **his own** home"; *Тэр гэр**т** харьсан* = "He went back to a home (whose, who knows)". The difference is real, and Mongolians hear it immediately.

**For body parts, the most natural way is body part + маань / тань + өвдөж байна.** *Толгой **маань** өвдөж байна* = "my head hurts". ⚠️ Saying *Би толгой өвдөж байна* sounds wrong — it's the head that hurts, not the person.

**Өвдөх = to hurt (body), өвчтэй = sick (state), эмнэлэг = hospital, эмч = doctor, эм = medicine.** Notice that *эм* (medicine), *эмч* (doctor) and *эмнэлэг* (hospital) share one root — the *-ч* suffix makes a person, the *-лэг* suffix makes a place. This pattern is widespread and helps you guess new words.
**Хэрэв … бол = "if … then".** *Хэрэв* goes in front, *бол* after the clause. The two bracket it, like English "if … then". ⚠️ *Хэрэв* can be left out; *бол* can't.

grammars.title: The reflexive suffix -аа: "one's own"
body: This is the suffix foreign speakers forget most often and native speakers notice most quickly. It attaches **after** the case suffix, and means the thing belongs to the subject of the sentence.
after: ⚠️ **The suffix works for any subject, not just "I".** *Би номоо уншина* (I read my book), *чи номоо унш* (you read your book), *тэр номоо уншсан* (she read her own book). One suffix handles everyone — once again, Mongolian refuses to change for the subject.

**When is it a must?** Whenever the thing belongs to the subject and that matters. For family members, personal things, home, work and home region, Mongolians **almost always** use it. When in doubt, add it — too much reflexive is far less jarring than too little.

grammars.title: Describing pain
body: Three patterns cover almost everything you need to say at a clinic. Learn all three as whole chunks.
after: ⚠️ **The last two rows can save your life and are worth memorizing before you travel.** Also write them down in Mongolian and keep the paper in your wallet — if you're unconscious, the paper speaks for you.

**Mongolia's health system provides free emergency care to anyone**, including foreigners. For further treatment, travel insurance is a must. Emergency numbers: **103** for an ambulance, **102** for the police, **101** for the fire service.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that **хэл means both "tongue" and "language"** — just like English "mother tongue", and like Latin *lingua*. *Монгол хэл* is literally "the Mongolian tongue". Likewise *зүрх* means both heart and courage: *зүрхтэй хүн* = a brave person (literally "a person with heart").

Notice the pattern for medicine names: **the illness takes -ын/-ийн + эм**. *Ханиад* (flu) → *ханиадны эм* (flu medicine). It's the possessive pattern you know from unit 2, and it works for almost every medicine. If you know the name of the illness, you can ask for its medicine.

blocks.title: Six sentences you need at the pharmacy
items: *Ханиадны эм байгаа юу?* — Do you have flu medicine?
*Жоргүй авч болох уу?* — Can I buy it without a prescription?
*Яаж уух вэ?* — How do I take it?
*Өдөрт хэдэн удаа уух вэ?* — How many times a day do I take it?
*Би пенициллинд харштай.* — I'm allergic to penicillin.
*Илүү хүчтэй эм байгаа юу?* — Do you have anything stronger?

sections.title: Sentences with the reflexive in daily life

head: Sentence
Meaning
Why reflexive
rows: I'm going back to my home.
I'm going back to my home region.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **The last row shows something important: the reflexive can also attach after the direction suffix *-руу*.** *Нутаг руу**гаа*** = to one's own home region. Mongolian stacks suffixes freely, always in a fixed order: **base → plural → case → reflexive**. Once you recognize this order, you can take apart a word of any length.

items: How many times a day do I take it?
